data.title: Onto Innovation stock jumps 13% on $1.1B backlog, upbeat outlook, AI demand
data.description:
Onto Innovation (ONTO) stock jumped over ~13% to ~$306 on Friday after the company reported a strong set of Q2 earnings and gave an optimistic outlook for the coming quarters. The rally pushed the stock's gain for the week to nearly 23%.

Moreover, the stock has been one of the best performers in the semiconductor sector this year, gaining 96.61% year to date, compared with the S&P 500 (SP500)'s 12.63% return in the same period.

The biggest reason behind Onto Innovation's price surge was a record second quarter with a revenue of $343.1M, up 35% from a year ago, while non-GAAP earnings rose to $1.93 per share from $1.25 last year.

The company said revenue, profit margins, and earnings all came in above the high end of its guidance.

Growth was driven by strong demand for AI-related semiconductor technologies. Revenue from advanced nodes jumped 50% from the previous quarter, while advanced packaging and specialty devices also reached record levels, supported by demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), 2.5D packaging, and silicon photonics.

Investors were also encouraged by the company's record backlog of more than $1.1B, providing better visibility into future sales.

Looking ahead, Onto Innovation expects Q3 revenue of $380M-$400M and non-GAAP EPS of $2.18-$2.38. Management also raised its second-half revenue growth outlook to 25% or more, saying strong AI demand could continue well into 2027.

The company also enjoys strong support from analysts. Wall Street has a 'Strong Buy' rating, while Seeking Alpha and the Quant system rate the stock 'Buy,' reflecting confidence in the company's growth outlook.

data.title: U.S. equities advanced after a weaker than forecasted payrolls report
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages traded towards the topside on Friday after July's nonfarm payrolls surprised to the downside, showing an unexpected contraction in employment.

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) was last +0.1%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) was last +0.5%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) was last +1%. 

From a sector-by-sector perspective, seven of the 11 S&P segments pushed up in the green and were led by consumer discretionary, while financials struggled the most. 

U.S. nonfarm payrolls declined by 23K in July, missing the +88K consensus and erasing the 20K increase in June, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. What's more, June's growth was scaled back by more than half from the initial print of 57K. Unemployment slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% in June, lower than the 4.2% consensus. 

“The weaker-than-expected jobs report likely doesn't change much for the Federal Reserve, as Chair Warsh is allowing the data to guide policy and the data as of now likely warrants keeping rates at current levels,” Brent Wilsey of Wilsey Asset Management stated. 

Treasury yields moved lower across the curve. The U.S. 2-Year Treasury yield (US2Y) dropped 4 basis points to 4.20%, the U.S. 10-Year Treasury yield (US10Y) slipped by 2 basis points to 4.65%, and the U.S. 30-Year Treasury yield (US30Y) was down 2 basis points to 5.20%. 

As for stocks that were on the move, shares of Airbnb (ABNB) advanced by 15.1%, while shares of The Trade Desk (TTD) fell 20.2%.

data.title: Interface signals FY2026 net sales of $1.455B-$1.485B with ~40.6% adjusted gross margin
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Interface, Inc. (TILE) Q2 2026

Management view

  • “Interface delivered another strong quarter, exceeding our expectations, achieving 4% year-over-year currency-neutral net sales growth… Growth was broad-based across regions, product categories and primary market segments,” said (President, CEO & Director Laurel Hurd). “Profitability also improved significantly this quarter, driven in part by the IEEPA tariff refunds we recognized. More importantly, continued operational execution improvements also contributed to margin expansion.”

  • “Noravant timber… is gaining momentum in the market… we’re seeing encouraging specification activity from leading design firms,” said (CEO Hurd). “We believe noravant represents a meaningful opportunity to further expand in Healthcare and other segments over time.”

  • “We’re continuing to invest in automation and robotics to improve efficiency and expand margins… investments are exceeding expectations,” said (CEO Hurd), pointing to robotics in Europe and Australia, “new packaging automation in Australia,” and “robotics in Germany to enhance efficiency in our rubber business.”

  • “Second quarter net sales were $395.7 million, up 5.4% as reported and 3.8% on a currency-neutral basis,” said (VP & CFO Bruce Hausman). “Second quarter adjusted gross profit margin was 45%, up 524 basis points… The remaining 393 basis points were driven by a $15.6 million benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds and represented approximately $0.19 of earnings per diluted share.”

Outlook

  • “With a healthy backlog, strong order momentum and the margin performance we achieved in the first half, we are raising our full year guidance,” said (CFO Hausman). “We are not assuming any additional refunds going forward.”

  • “For the third quarter of fiscal 2026, net sales of $370 million to $380 million; adjusted gross profit margin of approximately 40.8% of net sales; adjusted SG&A expenses of approximately $100 million; adjusted interest and other expenses of approximately $4 million,” said (CFO Hausman), adding “an adjusted effective income tax rate of approximately 27.5%” and “fully diluted weighted average share count of approximately 58.2 million shares.”

  • “For the full fiscal year of 2026… we anticipate net sales of $1.455 billion to $1.485 billion; adjusted gross profit margin of approximately 40.6% of net sales; adjusted SG&A expenses of approximately $395 million… adjusted interest and other expenses of approximately $15 million… an adjusted effective income tax rate of approximately 26% and capital expenditures of approximately $60 million,” said (CFO Hausman).

Financial results

  • “Second quarter adjusted operating income was $74.9 million… Second quarter adjusted net income was $51.5 million… Second quarter adjusted EBITDA was $87.7 million… and second quarter adjusted earnings per diluted share was $0.88,” said (CFO Hausman).

  • “We generated $38.4 million of cash from operating activities and capital expenditures were $12.2 million,” said (CFO Hausman). “We also repurchased $8.8 million of Interface common stock and paid our quarterly dividend.”

Q&A

  • Brian Biros, Thompson Research Group: “Can you talk about the margins for Q3 and Q4… the puts and takes?” VP Hausman: “It’s just the timing of the flow-through… we feel really good about gross margins going forward.”

  • Brian Biros, Thompson Research Group: asked whether the guidance raise was “just the Q2 beat.” CEO Hurd: “Nothing has really changed… We came in a little bit better in Q2.”

  • David S. MacGregor, Longbow Research: asked to “bridge… the 131 basis points.” VP Hausman: “The automation and robotics… are a large piece… these are durable and structural changes.”

  • Alexander Paris, Barrington Research: asked about tariff refunds and whether it was “one and done.” VP Hausman: “It was a onetime refund… we’re still subject to tariffs, and we’re still paying tariffs every single day going forward. And that’s baked into our guide.”

  • Reuben Garner, The Benchmark Company: asked about SG&A and freight inflation. VP Hausman: “The freight… lands on the cost of goods sold line… the increase… is mostly due to variable selling commissions… variable comp… and… foreign currency.”

Sentiment analysis

  • Analysts were slightly positive, with repeated emphasis on sustainability of gross margins, tariff mechanics, and operating expense discipline, including “a lot of focus around gross margins” (David S. MacGregor, Longbow Research) and scrutiny of the “one and done” nature of the refund (Alexander Paris, Barrington Research).

  • Management tone was positive and confident in prepared remarks and Q&A, using language such as “we feel really good” (VP Hausman) and “we’re committed to continuing margin expansion” (CEO Hurd), while also limiting forward assumptions: “We are not assuming any additional refunds going forward” (VP Hausman).

  • Versus last quarter, Q2 discussion shifted from potential refunds being “a really dynamic situation” (VP Hausman, Q1) to confirming receipt and financial impact: “a $15.6 million benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds” (VP Hausman, Q2).

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q2 emphasized margin expansion tied to a specific one-time item, while Q1 framed tariff refunds as uncertain: “There’s nothing assumed in our guide around the tariff refund” (VP Hausman, Q1) versus “we also recorded a $15.6 million tariff refund in the second quarter” (VP Hausman, Q2).

  • Segment growth mix shifted, with Q1 highlighting “Corporate office… billings were up 16%” (CEO Hurd, Q1) and Q2 calling out “Healthcare had a standout quarter with global billings up 19%” (CEO Hurd, Q2).

  • Backlog language stayed constructive but strengthened in magnitude: “Backlog… up 18% year-to-date” (CEO Hurd, Q1) versus “Backlog… up 22% year-to-date… giving us confidence to raise our full year guidance” (CEO Hurd, Q2).

Risks and concerns

  • “We’re seeing low single-digit inflation cost increases in our raw materials,” said (VP & CFO Hausman), adding that proactive pricing and inventory timing affects near-term margin cadence.

  • “We’re still subject to tariffs, and we’re still paying tariffs every single day going forward,” said (CFO Hausman), while noting the refund was “a onetime refund.”

Final takeaway

Interface’s management described Q2 as broad-based growth with sharply higher profitability, while tying a meaningful portion of margin upside to a one-time $15.6 million IEEPA tariff refund and highlighting continued structural gains from automation, mix, and pricing execution. The company raised full-year guidance and outlined Q3 and FY2026 targets, while repeatedly stressing it is “not assuming any additional refunds going forward” and that ongoing tariff and raw-material inflation pressures remain embedded in its outlook.

data.title: AEye reaffirms $30M-$35M 2026 cash use as it ramps output for 2H
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: AEye, Inc. (LIDR) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "I'm excited to report that our overall momentum continued in the second quarter... having grown to our highest level of engagement yet" (CEO & Chairman Matthew Fisch). "I'm pleased to announce that we have been selected as the preferred lidar vendor for a groundbreaking sports analytics provider."
  • "Q2 revenue grew approximately 9x year-over-year and roughly 100% quarter-over-quarter, marking our fourth consecutive quarter of growth" (CEO & Chairman Fisch). "Proof-of-concept programs from revenue-generating customers grew to 25 from 21 since our last earnings call and both engagements and quote activity increased approximately 25% and 40% quarter-over-quarter, respectively."
  • "Defense continues to be our most active vertical with engagements doubling quarter-over-quarter" (CEO & Chairman Fisch). "Our lead defense customer placed its third consecutive paid order this quarter" and "our partnership with Fintech... continues to actively promote and ship Apollo to its customers."
  • "Apollo was recently validated on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor" (CEO & Chairman Fisch). "OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers building on the NVIDIA DRIVE platform can source Apollo as a prequalified sensor, reducing integration risk and shortening the path from system design to deployment."
  • "Second quarter revenue was $202,000" (CFO, Treasurer & Chief Business Development Officer Conor Tierney). "Two components drove the quarter" including "$30,000 of contract development revenue from customer-funded engineering work."

Outlook

  • "We're reaffirming our 2026 full year cash use outlook of $30 million to $35 million" (CFO Tierney). "We expect second half consumption to run higher than the first half as we start to ramp the manufacturing build."
  • "We have begun ramping our output to match our forecast of increased customer demand in the second half of the year" (CEO & Chairman Fisch). In Q&A, he added: "We're just focused maniacally on quarter-on-quarter growth... The last 4 quarters. we've doubled quarter-on-quarter consistently. We aim to continue down that path here in the back half of the year."
  • "We announced one commercial win. But we think we're on the one yard line here with a few other customer announcements" (CFO Tierney). "We expect to probably getting some news out here in the next few months or so."

Financial Results

  • "Second quarter revenue was $202,000" (CFO Tierney), including product revenue where "repeat orders from our lead defense customer continued to grow in size quarter-over-quarter" and "we started shipping units to Alive3D," plus "$30,000 of contract development revenue."
  • "GAAP operating expenses were $10.6 million versus $8.9 million in the first quarter" (CFO Tierney). "Non-GAAP operating expenses... were $8.2 million compared to $7.4 million."
  • "We reported a GAAP net loss of $10 million or $0.22 per share" and "on a non-GAAP basis, our net loss was $7.6 million or $0.17 per share" (CFO Tierney).
  • "Second quarter cash consumption was $7.5 million compared to $9.2 million in the first quarter" and "we ended the quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of approximately $71.5 million" (CFO Tierney).

Q&A

  • Richard Shannon, Craig-Hallum: asked to "quantify" the 2H output ramp and which end markets drive it; CEO & Chairman Fisch said, "we're fully loaded with 25 different customer programs" and "we expect that to continue through the back half of the year," while CFO Tierney added, "we think we're on the one yard line here with a few other customer announcements."
  • Richard Shannon, Craig-Hallum: asked about contract development revenue end market and future contribution; CFO Tierney said, "this customer was in the aerospace and defense sector" and "we're going to see contract development revenues become a more meaningful number on our P&L," while CEO & Chairman Fisch said, "the customer is putting skin in the game... and that comes along with product sales as well."
  • Richard Shannon, Craig-Hallum: asked about auto RFIs/RFQs and timing; CEO & Chairman Fisch said, "we had a new evaluation start" and "we've had an RFQ come in," but "automotive programs take a lot longer time to process."
  • Charles Fratt, Alliance Global Partners: asked what attracts and retains customers; CEO & Chairman Fisch said, "we'll call it the 1 kilometer sensing range headline" and "we give that flexibility through the software defined" approach, adding, "there is some fierce competition" and "that's why we won that project."
  • Charles Fratt, Alliance Global Partners: asked about defense interest and broadening use cases; CEO & Chairman Fisch said Q2 saw "a very large influx of counter UAS" and described it as "counter drone detection," while CFO Tierney added, "we may initially engage with the customer about one particular use case" and then "that may lead to opportunities elsewhere."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts slightly positive: Richard Shannon said, "Congrats on a really nice quarter" and sought more detail on the 2H ramp; questions focused on production scaling, contract development revenue durability, and defense demand broadening.
  • Management positive and confident: CEO & Chairman Fisch said, "As a company, we're hitting our stride" and later, "we're really excited about what's around the corner in the back half of the year," while CFO Tierney said, "conversion is no longer theoretical."
  • Current vs. previous quarter tone: Q1 opened with "steady execution, no surprises" (CEO & Chairman Fisch), while Q2 emphasized new proof points such as "selected as the preferred lidar vendor" for Alive3D and being "validated on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor" (CEO & Chairman Fisch).

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Pipeline and conversion language sharpened: Q1 highlighted "more commercial engagement than at any point in our history" and customers rising "from 15 to 21" (CEO & Chairman Fisch), while Q2 reported "proof-of-concept programs... grew to 25 from 21" and stated "repeat business is now a pattern rather than an exception" (CFO Tierney).
  • New revenue stream and vertical: Q2 added "$30,000 of contract development revenue" (CFO Tierney) and announced sports analytics with Alive3D; Q1 discussion centered on expanding engagements and partner ecosystem without citing contract development revenue.
  • Production posture shifted: Q2 said, "We have begun ramping our output" (CEO & Chairman Fisch); Q1 framed manufacturing as a strength and highlighted a capital runway narrative but did not describe a production ramp.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Automotive programs take a lot longer time to process" (CEO & Chairman Fisch), and OEM evaluations were described as a "long process."
  • "We expect second half consumption to run higher than the first half" as manufacturing builds ramp (CFO Tierney).
  • Cost variability was flagged through higher operating expenses tied to "nonrecurring engineering, tooling and test costs" and "noncash stock-based compensation" (CFO Tierney).
  • Competitive intensity was acknowledged in sports analytics: "there is some fierce competition" (CEO & Chairman Fisch).

Final Takeaway

Management described Q2 as an inflection in commercial validation, pointing to Alive3D selecting Apollo in sports analytics, Apollo being validated on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, and defense remaining the most active vertical with repeat orders and expanding use cases. The company reiterated its $30 million to $35 million 2026 cash use outlook while preparing for higher second-half cash consumption tied to manufacturing ramp, and emphasized that repeat business, contract development revenue, and multiple near-term customer announcements are intended to support continued quarter-on-quarter revenue growth.

data.title: Voya says Toms Capital materials contain inaccurate, misleading statements
data.description:
Voya Financial (VOYA) said Toms Capital materials contain "inaccurate and misleading" statements and reproduce media reports that contain false information about the company.

"These materials describe a fictitious shareholder meeting in a manner and format that is liable to confuse and deceive our investors," Voya said in a  statement on Friday.

The response comes after Toms, which has a 4.5% stake in Voya (VOYA), on Thursday announced it filed proxy materials to provide holders with the opportunity to consider and vote on a non-binding resolution. The non-binding resolution allows shareholders to convey unequivocally that they “no longer continue to have confidence" in the board and management of Voya.

Voya (VOYA)  advised its holders that there is no upcoming meeting and there are no matters for holders to vote on for which proxies could be solicited. Voya also highlighted that it held its annual meeting in May.

Toms in June repeated a call for Voya (VOYA) to explore its options, including a sale of the company, and engage with interested buyers. Reports in April indicated that Toms had taken a stake in Voya (VOYA) and was pushing for the company to put itself up for sale or offload its underperforming health insurer arm.

data.title: Ardelyx signals lower 2026 IBSRELA guidance to $350M-$370M while revising 2026 opex to below $500M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Ardelyx (ARDX) Q2 2026

Management View

  • “In Q2, IBSRELA and XPHOZAH generated a combined revenue of $118 million, up 31% year-over-year, the largest quarterly revenue in our company's history.” (President, CEO & Director Michael Raab)
  • “Growth in the second quarter was robust and yet performance fell short of our expectations.” (President, CEO & Director Raab)
  • “Payers have implemented significant hurdles that impacted new patient starts and access to IBSRELA.” (President, CEO & Director Raab)
  • “On June 26, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the district court's dismissal of our lawsuit against CMS… we have determined that we will no longer pursue further litigation on this matter.” (President, CEO & Director Raab)
  • “We are a well-funded, self-sustaining, high-growth company on the path to sustained profitability in 2027 and beyond.” (President, CEO & Director Raab)
  • “We continue to see strong growth in refills and total prescriptions, reaching our highest demand quarter to date.” (Chief Commercial Officer Eric Foster)
  • “Our data shows that when a prescription goes through the IPN, it results in higher fulfillment rates, faster fills, and in 1 additional refill per patient on an annual basis.” (Chief Commercial Officer Foster)
  • “Our second quarter 2026 financial results reflect the ongoing transformation of Ardelyx into a financially strong organization… we maintained our focus of turning disciplined capital allocation into a clear strategic advantage.” (Chief Financial Officer Sue Hohenleitner)

Outlook

  • “We have made the prudent decision to lower our full-year 2026 guidance for IBSRELA to a range of $350 million to $370 million.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “We are reiterating our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to be between $110 million and $120 million.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “We are revising our 2026 OPEX guidance to be below $500 million.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “Let me be clear. We are still on a path to achieve $1 billion in revenue for IBSRELA. However, with the 2026 revenue revision, we are evaluating the evolving market dynamics and the impact on the timing of this achievement.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “Therefore, it is prudent to revisit our internal assumptions and pull our $750 million revenue guidance.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)

Financial Results

  • “In the second quarter, our total product revenue was $118 million compared to $90 million in the same period last year.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “Our Q2 2026 revenues of $86.2 million increased 33% compared to Q2 of 2025.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “Revenues for XPHOZAH during the quarter was $31.9 million, an increase of 27% compared to the second quarter of 2025.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “R&D expenses for the quarter were $26.1 million compared to $15.7 million for the same period in 2025… for the ongoing ACCEL Phase III clinical trial in CIC.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “SG&A expenses were $101.4 million for the quarter compared to $84 million for the same period in 2025.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “Net loss for the quarter was $16.7 million, compared to a net loss of $19.1 million for the same period in 2025.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “We ended the second quarter with $281.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • “During the second quarter, we drew down $50 million from our existing arrangement with SLR.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)

Q&A

  • Ryan (on for Roanna Ruiz), Leerink Partners: Asked what demand metrics support the revised IBSRELA guidance and what “pushes and pulls” are embedded; Chief Commercial Officer Foster said “we continue to see really strong refills and total prescriptions” and highlighted IPN benefits including “higher fulfillment rates” and “1 more refill,” while Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner said “we've seen the current performance… we know the friction… and we have baked that into the guidance.”
  • Yuchen Ding, Jefferies: Asked what payer hurdles are (step edits vs. blocks) and requested quantitative fill/fulfillment details; Chief Commercial Officer Foster said payers are adding “more step edits” and “more stringent prior authorizations,” describing “a slowing of the new patient starts,” while President, CEO & Director Raab said “it is the extent of the step edits… [that] was not something that one would anticipate.”
  • Daniel Chon (for Chris Raymond), Raymond James: Asked about BD strategy amid industry M&A; President, CEO & Director Raab said “we are looking at opportunities every day” and added tenapanor IP “gives us runway… that my guess is not fully appreciated through 2042.”
  • Matthew Caufield, H.C. Wainwright: Asked whether IBSRELA access challenges worsened; President, CEO & Director Raab said the company previously avoided rebating “until there was a need to” and is starting payer discussions, while Chief Commercial Officer Foster said “the speed and the extent” of stricter PAs and step edits “we're not really anticipating… as quickly as it was.”
  • Laura Chico, Wedbush: Asked about the implied second-half ramp and ANDA/IP barriers; Chief Commercial Officer Foster said FRMs address “both… new patients as well as… patients… working through the process,” while President, CEO & Director Raab said “we won't go into specifics as to whether or not we've gotten challenges” and cited non-absorbed drug complexity, FDA guidance barriers, and confidence in the “'299 estate… through 2042 and potentially beyond.”
  • Yigal Nochomovitz, Citi: Asked if IBS-C payer pushback is broad and why XPHOZAH’s $750 million guide was withdrawn; Chief Commercial Officer Foster said the company is seeing “more stringent prior authorization criteria” and step edits across “a meaningful amount” of payers, while President, CEO & Director Raab tied XPHOZAH uncertainty to “the end of the TDAPA period,” a proposed “phosphorus QIP,” and wanting to “take a step back from the $750 million.”
  • Julian Harrison, BTIG: Asked profitability timing and CIC Phase III framing; Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner said “we will be income positive next year” and noted “our cost structure will level out,” while President, CEO & Director Raab said CIC has “great synergy with the sales force that we currently have” and “we're on track to deliver data… in the timeframe that you just articulated.”
  • Caroline Palomeque, Ladenburg: Asked coupon/discounting impact on gross-to-net (GTN); Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner said “our guidance on GTN… low to mid-30s… still continues to be the case,” citing mix, IRA inflation rebates, co-pay, and distribution discounts.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative, with repeated pressure on the IBSRELA slowdown mechanics and quantification (e.g., “Can you give more color on what those hurdles are?” and requests for “quantitative metrics”). (Yuchen Ding, Jefferies)
  • Management: neutral to slightly positive in framing demand strength while acknowledging access friction (e.g., “performance fell short of our expectations” alongside “IBSRELA demand is strong”). (President, CEO & Director Raab)
  • Versus last quarter: Q2 carried more defensive clarification around access (“To be clear, IBSRELA demand is strong”) and more caution on long-term targets (withdrawing XPHOZAH’s $750 million), while Q1 emphasized confidence and reiterated long-term goals (e.g., “we remain on track to deliver at least $1 billion in annual revenue in 2029”). (President, CEO & Director Raab)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Guidance shifted materially: Q1 reiterated IBSRELA “between $410 million and $430 million” and in Q2 it was lowered to “$350 million to $370 million.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • Long-term framing changed for XPHOZAH: in Q1, Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner said “yes, we will reiterate the $750 million,” while in Q2 she said it was “prudent… [to] pull our $750 million revenue guidance.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • Cost guidance tightened: Q1 guided “about $520 million in total OpEx,” while Q2 revised to “below $500 million.” (Chief Financial Officer Hohenleitner)
  • Commercial narrative shifted from seasonality/storm disruption in Q1 to payer restrictions in Q2, with management highlighting “more step edits” and “more stringent prior authorizations.” (Chief Commercial Officer Foster)

Risks and Concerns

  • “Significant payer hurdles… impacted new patient starts and access to IBSRELA,” including “more step edits” and “more stringent prior authorizations,” with mitigation centered on doubling the field reimbursement team, expanding the sales force to “144 representatives,” and pushing scripts through the IPN for higher fulfillment. (Chief Commercial Officer Foster)
  • “Oral-only phosphate-lowering drugs remain in the bundle” after the D.C. Circuit decision, and the company said it “will no longer pursue further litigation,” while still aiming to keep XPHOZAH available amid uncertainty tied to TDAPA transition and policy measures like a proposed phosphorus QIP. (President, CEO & Director Raab)

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized record quarterly revenue and continued demand strength across IBSRELA and XPHOZAH, but characterized Q2 as below internal expectations due to payer-driven access friction slowing IBSRELA new starts. The company lowered full-year 2026 IBSRELA guidance to $350 million-$370 million, held XPHOZAH’s 2026 range at $110 million-$120 million, reduced 2026 OPEX guidance to below $500 million, and withdrew the prior $750 million XPHOZAH long-term target to reassess evolving dialysis reimbursement and policy dynamics. Management continued to point to profitability in 2027 while investing in access infrastructure, commercial execution, and the ACCEL Phase III CIC program.

data.title: Magazine Luiza S.A. reports Q2 results
Verastem outlines October VS-7375 response-rate update while targeting LGSOC self-sustainability by end of 2026
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Verastem Oncology (VSTM) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Daniel Paterson said the quarter delivered both commercial and pipeline momentum: "We delivered a strong second quarter with meaningful progress across both our commercial business and pipeline" and reported "net product revenues of $25.1 million," which he said reflected execution that is "putting us back on track and reinforcing the long-term opportunity for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK."
  • Paterson highlighted balance-sheet actions and timing: "We also strengthened the balance sheet with a non-dilutive royalty financing agreement with Oberland Capital to secure up to $75 million in funding, of which we expect to draw $50 million at closing," and added that "a $15 million milestone payment from Secura Bio" together represented "the incremental $90 million in non-dilutive funding" that "strengthens our balance sheet" and "preserves strategic flexibility."
  • On the LGSOC launch trajectory, Paterson said, "we continue to expect the LGSOC business will become self-sustaining by the end of 2026," and described a Q1-to-Q2 rebound: "Since the first quarter, we've seen a meaningful rebound with significant quarter-over-quarter growth" driven by "growing physician confidence," earlier-line use, and "increasing patient refills."
  • Chief Commercial Officer Daniel Lyons said the launch focus remains: "driving consistent new patient demand, expanding use earlier in the treatment journey, and helping patients to stay on therapy," and added, "we drove meaningful growth in the adoption of the CO-PACK, and we are seeing that momentum continue in Q3."
  • CFO Daniel Calkins said spending discipline remains intact: "we expect SG&A expenses to remain roughly the same on a quarterly basis throughout 2026," and stated, "we believe we have sufficient capital to fund operations into the second half of 2027."

Outlook

  • Paterson laid out second-half priorities: "Drive strong execution of our commercial strategy to expand adoption of AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK, complete enrollment in our three Phase II registration-directed VS-7375 trials, and prepare to initiate our three Phase III trials for VS-7375."
  • On the next clinical catalyst, Paterson said, "In October, we expect to provide a more comprehensive data set for VS-7375, including response rates across our three lead tumor types, pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers, with approximately 20 patients in each, as well as an early look at durability."
  • In Q&A, President of Development Michael Glen Kauffman reinforced the accelerated-approval framing: "30% is a great metric in this disease. Six months is also terrific," adding that regulators consider "both activity as well as the safety and tolerability profile."

Financial Results

  • Calkins reported $25.1 million in net product revenue, $3.8 million in product cost of sales, and "$15 million in license revenue" tied to COPIKTRA, which he said was triggered when "cumulative worldwide net sales of COPIKTRA surpassing $200 million during the second quarter of 2026."
  • Calkins reported operating expenses of $41.3 million in R&D and $27.4 million in SG&A, and said non-GAAP adjusted net loss was $30.6 million, or $0.31 per diluted share.
  • On liquidity, Calkins said cash, equivalents, and investments were $136.4 million at quarter-end; he added, "our pro forma cash balance at the end of the second quarter is $201.4 million" when including the Oberland closing draw and the COPIKTRA milestone.

Q&A

  • Eric Schmidt, Cantor Fitzgerald: asked about G12D partnership activity; CEO Paterson said, "We continue to work on the Erasca partnership" and cited "considerable inbound interest from strategics," adding the new financing "gives us a lot more strategic flexibility to not have to rush." CFO Calkins, on margins, said, "Yes, I think that is a reasonable run" given cost of sales is "still continues to be royalty-based."
  • Michelle Boisvert, Guggenheim: asked whether "30% overall response rate and six months durability" remains the right bar; President Kauffman said, "We think that's generally a very good guidepost" and emphasized tolerability tradeoffs versus rash/stomatitis.
  • Joshua Wolfson, RBC: asked about translating GenFleet China ORR to the U.S.; CEO Paterson said, "the most important benchmarks are going to be the U.S. data" and President Kauffman added, "Direct translation, probably not direct, but within the ballpark."
  • Faisal Khurshid, Jefferies: asked whether CO-PACK growth was new starts vs. duration; CCO Lyons said, "It's a bit of both," citing "meaningful increase in new prescribers and new accounts" plus encouraging refill execution.
  • Graig Suvannavejh, Mizuho: asked what will drive sales and how VS-7375 differentiates; CCO Lyons said, "you need all three" (new starts, earlier line, persistence), while CEO Paterson said versus panRAS they intend "better efficacy and significantly better tolerability," and President Kauffman said, "We have no rash and no mucositis" and PK "continues to climb" from 400 to 600 to 900.
  • Andres Maldonado, H.C. Wainwright: asked about earlier-line prescribing and CRC strategy; CEO Paterson said, "we don't intend to develop it as a single agent. It's going to be with an EGFR inhibitor," and CCO Lyons said earlier-line movement is occurring "not only in the academic, but also in the community" with dose interruptions expected but managed.
  • Jeet Mukherjee, BTIG: asked PRMT5 strategy and FDA bar; CEO Paterson said, "we're exploring all options," while President Kauffman said, "The FDA has never told us what they need" but called "30% ORR with at least six months durability" a "great rule of thumb."
  • Matthew Venezia, Alliance Global Partners: asked how physicians choose between panRAS and trials; President Kauffman said the discussion is "an efficacy and a tolerability discussion" and added, "they would recommend for a G12D patient that they go on to a G12D specific drug" given tolerability concerns with panRAS.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, repeatedly referencing a "strong quarter" and probing durability/competitiveness (e.g., Guggenheim asked if the "competitive landscape in PDAC" changes what’s needed).
  • Management’s tone was positive and confident in prepared remarks (Paterson: "strong second quarter"), while remaining measured in Q&A on partnering timing (Paterson: "it's really a judgment call on how early or late you do a partnership") and relying on rule-of-thumb approval thresholds (Kauffman: "The FDA has never told us what they need").
  • Versus last quarter, Q2 messaging shifted from explaining "seasonal headwinds" and launch fixes to emphasizing a rebound (Paterson: "meaningful rebound") and incremental non-dilutive capital that reduces near-term financing pressure.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • The biggest change in emphasis was commercial momentum: Q1 discussed insurance/weather headwinds and later-line discontinuations; Q2 stressed that "the changes we made are having an impact" and highlighted increased refills and earlier-line use.
  • Capital strategy shifted from intent to find nondilutive options in Q1 to announcing a specific facility in Q2: "up to $75 million" with an expected "$50 million" draw at closing, plus the $15 million milestone.
  • The VS-7375 narrative moved from describing Phase II initiations and dose work in Q1 to setting a defined data event in Q2: "response rates" across three tumor types expected in October.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management cited launch execution risks tied to real-world persistence and line of therapy, emphasizing mitigation through field support to "help patients stay on therapy" and active adverse-event management.
  • On VS-7375 differentiation risk in a crowded landscape, CEO Paterson framed competitive priorities as "better efficacy and significantly better tolerability," while President Kauffman highlighted class-related tolerability concerns (rash, mucositis/stomatitis) and stated, "We have no rash and no mucositis."
  • On partnering/financing uncertainty, Paterson pointed to timing tradeoffs and said the new funding provides flexibility to "not have to rush into something nor rush into an equity financing."

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a commercial re-acceleration for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK alongside a clearer catalyst path for VS-7375, anchored by an October update with response rates across pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cohorts. Leadership also emphasized added financial flexibility via the Oberland royalty financing and the COPIKTRA milestone, while reiterating the goal for the LGSOC franchise to be self-sustaining by the end of 2026 and for current capital to fund operations into the second half of 2027.

data.title: Weave anticipates $273M-$275M 2026 revenue while raising operating income outlook to $12M-$14M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Weave Communications (WEAV) Q2 2026

Management View

  • Brett White (CEO & Director) said, "We've delivered strong results in the second quarter." He reported "Total revenue was $67.5 million, 15.5% growth over last year," and added that "Revenue retention measured on a quarterly basis also improved sequentially" and the company "added the most new locations ever in a single quarter, both on a gross and net basis."

  • White highlighted vertical performance, saying, "Dental, our largest vertical, had a strong quarter," and described specialty medical progress: "we released a significantly deeper integration with the athenaOne platform and joined athenahealth's Marketplace, making our innovative solutions available to more than 160,000 specialty medical providers."

  • On profitability and go-to-market efficiency, White said, "sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue was down sequentially" and "we expanded our operating margin to almost 5%, up sharply from roughly breakeven in the same quarter last year." He also flagged execution friction during a sales transition: "it took time to calibrate the lead distribution with the appropriate execution, resulting in bookings slightly below our expectation despite very strong demand."

  • Jason Christiansen (Chief Financial Officer) said, "The second quarter of 2026 was a solid quarter for Weave with continued revenue growth and much improved operating income," and noted a "slight headwind to Q2 revenue was a quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year decrease in onboarding revenue due to lower setup fees," adding, "Moving forward, we are renewing our focus on consistently collecting these onetime setup fees."

Outlook

  • Christiansen guided full-year 2026 revenue to "the range of $273 million to $275 million," saying it "reflects the impact of the go-to-market transition adjustment period" described by White.

  • Christiansen raised profitability expectations, saying, "we are raising our non-GAAP operating income guidance" and now expects "$12 million to $14 million," tying the change to "improvements in operating efficiency" from go-to-market initiatives.

  • For Q3 2026, Christiansen projected revenue of "$68.6 million to $69.6 million" and operating income of "$3 million to $4 million," and provided expected share count of "approximately 80.2 million shares" for Q3.

  • Compared with Q1 2026, the company’s full-year revenue outlook moved from "$275 million to $278 million" to "$273 million to $275 million," while full-year non-GAAP operating income outlook moved from "$10.5 million to $13.5 million" to "$12 million to $14 million."

Financial Results

  • Christiansen reported gross profit of "$49 million" and gross margin of "72.6%," and said sequential gross margin pressure reflected "increased usage fees for messaging and true-up invoices on certain vendor agreements" plus "an increase in credit card fees" tied to annual prepay cohorts.

  • Christiansen reported retention of "GRR was 89% and NRR was 92%," and emphasized that reported retention is "a weighted average of the previous 12 months monthly retention rates" and "it can take multiple quarters for improvements to show through in reported metrics."

  • Christiansen reported operating income of "$3.2 million" and said it "exceeded the top end of our guidance," adding that sales and marketing efficiency was a key driver as sales and marketing expense was "$25.8 million or 38% of revenue."

  • On cash generation, Christiansen said Weave ended with "$78.5 million in cash and short-term investments," with "cash from operating activities in Q2" of "$10.2 million" and "free cash flow" of "$8.7 million," adding, "We were free cash flow positive for the first half of 2026."

Q&A

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked how "record gross in net locations" and payments growth reconcile with a "lower growth outlook"; Jason Christiansen (CFO): said the impact stems from the May-to-July sales transition where "demand remained very strong" but lead distribution issues will "flow through in the back half of the year"; Brett White (CEO): added, "bookings shortfalls in May, June and July" will show up in "Q3" and "into Q4."

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked about May-to-July linearity, Q4 improvement assumptions, and sales team sizing; Brett White (CEO): said inbound verticalization is already showing "positive results," while outbound "got disrupted May to July" and the company "completed the transition first week in August"; on headcount, he stated, "the team size is smaller" and some sellers moved into SDR roles.

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked about specialty medical opportunity from athenahealth integration and upsell; Brett White (CEO): said, "Getting a deeper integration into athenahealth is huge" and described moving from "1 to 4" on integration levels; Jason Christiansen (CFO): explained Level 4 brings "read and write capabilities across multiple tables" and said integrated areas are already showing improved ASPs.

  • Hannah Rudoff, Piper Sandler: asked how long go-to-market disruption could persist and confidence in the guide; Jason Christiansen (CFO): said guidance reflects "our best thinking" and the accelerated cutover should have the business "back to executing" within "the next couple of months."

  • Hannah Rudoff, Piper Sandler: asked if demand weakened via sales cycles or budget scrutiny; Brett White (CEO): said, "I haven't seen any slacking a slackening of the demand environment" and added the disruption "was not demand related at all," also noting, "we announced a partnership with the American Dental Association... and it's doing really well."

  • J. Lane, Stifel: asked what drove stronger dental net adds and sustainability; Brett White (CEO): attributed it to focus from verticalizing inbound sales and marketing; Jason Christiansen (CFO): cited ADA partnership and said the company views the period as "a ripple in the path."

  • Mark Schappel, Loop Capital Markets: asked how AI engagement translates into financial results (ARPU/retention/revenue); Brett White (CEO): said AI modules are monetized "additionally and/or... part of an upsell" and also make Weave "stickier" and "easier to sell"; Jason Christiansen (CFO): differentiated AI features that are not explicitly monetized versus "net new incremental capabilities like AI receptionist"; White added that AI-driven workflows can expand "payments volume" and said, "we've got accelerating payments volume growth."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analyst tone was slightly negative to neutral, focusing on guide reset durability and execution risk around sales model changes, with repeated probing on the "lower growth outlook" and how long disruption could persist.

  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more explanatory in Q&A, repeatedly characterizing the issue as execution rather than demand; White said, "I haven't seen any slacking a slackening of the demand environment," while Christiansen emphasized the guide reflects "our best thinking" after accelerating the transition.

  • Versus Q1 2026, management language shifted from emphasizing repeated guidance outperformance (Q1: "Both revenue and profitability came in above the high end of our guidance") to emphasizing a transition-related adjustment (Q2: "resulting in bookings slightly below our expectation") alongside a higher operating income outlook.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • The biggest change was guidance direction: Q1 raised full-year revenue to "$275 million to $278 million," while Q2 reduced it to "$273 million to $275 million" and explicitly tied the change to the "go-to-market transition adjustment period" and "bookings shortfalls" during May to July.

  • Profit focus intensified: Q2 highlighted a sequential decline in sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue and raised full-year operating income guidance to "$12 million to $14 million," compared with "$10.5 million to $13.5 million" in Q1.

  • Strategic emphasis moved from product rollout timing in Q1 (omnichannel AI Receptionist broader availability discussed) to execution and organizational design in Q2, including inbound verticalization and completing the outbound SDR transition in early August.

  • Analyst questioning in Q1 centered more on AI Receptionist pricing and NRR mechanics, while Q2 concentrated on the revenue outlook reset and the operational impact of go-to-market changes.

Risks and Concerns

  • Christiansen identified onboarding revenue pressure from "lower setup fees" and said Weave is "renewing our focus" on collecting setup fees going forward.

  • Christiansen cited gross margin pressures from "increased usage fees for messaging" and "true-up invoices on certain vendor agreements," plus higher credit card fees from annual prepay cohorts.

  • White described execution risk in the sales transition, saying lead calibration issues caused "bookings slightly below our expectation" and that the impact is reflected in the revenue outlook.

  • White also highlighted unrealized value in AI-driven opportunities, noting call intelligence surfaced "810,000 unscheduled opportunities" and said "Only a portion of these opportunities were acted upon by staff," framing AI receptionist as a tool to close that gap.

Final Takeaway

Management described Q2 as a quarter of record location additions, expanding operating profitability, and accelerating AI engagement, while also acknowledging that a May-to-July outbound sales transition created a bookings shortfall that is now embedded in a lowered full-year revenue range. The company paired that revenue reset with higher full-year operating income guidance, attributing the profitability lift to sales and marketing efficiency gains and a faster completion of the SDR-led outbound model in early August, alongside continued investment in deeper vertical integrations such as athenahealth and monetized AI modules like AI Receptionist and Call Intelligence.
